name: Example: Integrating a Product of Sine and Cosine
worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+4x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-4x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}(-1-1)+\frac{1}{4}(-1-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
